title: Who’s Really Making the Call? Humans Step Into AI’s Work
part1: When you ask AI to make a phone call, who is the main player in that call? If we compare it to a play, AI is the name on the poster, while a human is the one who says the lines on the phone. In a test involving some calls made through Muse, trained human contract workers—not AI—made the calls and finished the conversations with the people they called.
part2:
Imagine a little scene where you ask a robot butler, “Make a phone call.” If you heard a human voice on the other end, wouldn’t you want to ask, “How much of the job is the butler doing?” The point is not so much that a human helps, but whether users are clearly told about it. A Meta vice president admitted that it was a mistake to start testing calls made by contract workers without explaining it properly.

Now, let’s put the laughter aside for a moment. The concern is how information is handled. Making a phone call may require the user’s information. Meta employees raised privacy concerns that the information might be shared with human contract workers by mistake. But this is about concerns being raised; it does not mean that a large-scale information leak happened.
part3:
When you ask AI to do something for you, don’t you care about more than just convenience? Don’t you also wonder, “Who actually does it?” If you ask it to call on your behalf, is the other person speaking to AI or a human, and what information will be shared? This is a little different from whether AI can talk just like a human. If you don’t know who has which role, it can be hard to watch the play with peace of mind. If a person is involved, telling you about it may be part of the service.

Meta has put its human concierge feature on hold for now. It stopped that feature, not Muse as a whole.
in_one_line: In a Muse test, human contractors—not AI—made some calls, and Meta has paused the feature.
